intuition: A clockwise rotation can be done in two simple steps. First swap rows and columns by reflecting cells across the main diagonal. Then reverse each row. For example, the old top-left cell ends at the top-right. Both steps change the existing matrix without allocating another matrix.

First transpose across the main diagonal, which exchanges row and column coordinates. Then reverse every row, turning the new column r into n-1-r. Their composition is precisely the clockwise mapping. Reversing before transposing would instead compose the transformations in a different order.

Transpose only entries above the diagonal, so each mirrored pair is exchanged once. Row reversal similarly swaps only opposite positions until its pointers meet. No additional matrix is needed, and every original value survives exactly once in the caller’s original matrix object.

steps: Begin with [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]. Swap positions (0,1) and (1,0), exchanging values 2 and 4.
Swap positions (0,2) and (2,0), exchanging 3 and 7. Swap positions (1,2) and (2,1), exchanging 6 and 8.
The transpose is now [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]. Diagonal values 1,5,9 have not moved yet.
Reverse the first row by exchanging 1 and 7, giving [7,4,1].
Reverse the second row to [8,5,2] and the third row to [9,6,3].
The original matrix now equals [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]], the required clockwise rotation.

codeNotes.note: Visit only the upper triangle. Visiting the mirrored lower entries later would swap each pair back and undo the transpose.
Tuple assignment preserves both original values while exchanging them, requiring no allocated replacement matrix.
Each opposite row pair is swapped once. Stopping when the pointers meet prevents reversing the same pair twice.

keyDecision: Swap each diagonal pair once, then reverse every row.

concept.question: Can a quarter-turn be built from two reflections?
intuition: Copying every cell to a new matrix would make rotation easy but violates the in-place requirement. A rotation has a useful geometric decomposition that only exchanges existing cells.

First reflect the matrix across its main diagonal, exchanging row and column roles. Then reverse each row. Together, these reflections move every original cell to exactly its clockwise quarter-turn destination.
concept.observation: Exchange each off-diagonal pair once, then reverse each row.
approach: Reflect across the top-left to bottom-right diagonal.
Reverse the order of cells within every row.
Keep the same matrix while its values move to their rotated positions.
concept.correctness: Diagonal reflection moves a cell’s row coordinate to its column coordinate and vice versa. Reversing a reflected row then mirrors the new column coordinate across the row width. This is exactly the clockwise rotation rule for every cell. Both operations exchange values inside the original square matrix, preserving all cells and the matrix identity.

complexity.explanation: Visit a constant number of times for each cell, giving work proportional to the square’s cell count. Only temporary exchange values are needed, so auxiliary memory is constant.

pitfalls: Reflect each off-diagonal pair only once.
Reverse rows after reflecting, to rotate clockwise.
Modify the original matrix rather than returning a separate copy.
